Key Takeaways

Oracle stock is down 55.0% over the past year, closing at $126.16 on October 23, even though Oracle beat Wall Street's adjusted EPS estimate in each of the last four quarters.

Fiscal first-quarter revenue rose 30% to $19.3B, while free cash flow came in at negative $5B.

Analysts expect revenue to climb from $90.42B in fiscal 2027 to $183.81B in fiscal 2029.

Next test: Investor Day on October 28.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stock is down 55.0% over the past year, closing at $126.16 on October 23. Over the same stretch, Oracle beat Wall Street's adjusted EPS estimate in four straight quarters.

That gap is the story. By my math, Oracle stock started the period near $280, so a year of beats still left the shares at less than half that price. The pressure came from how Oracle funds its AI data centers, not from demand for them.

How Oracle Stock Gave Back Its June Rally
ORCL Stock Price: 1-Year (TIKR)

The first leg was a slide from the low $280s in early November to around $140 by late January. The bigger swing came later. Oracle posted fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted EPS of $2.11 on June 10 against a $1.96 estimate, and the stock peaked near $248 that month before falling to about $116 by late July. In between, S&P Global cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk.

Oracle Stock's September: A Beat, Then New Mexico

Oracle's fiscal first-quarter results on September 10 showed revenue up 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud infrastructure revenue up 121% to $7.4 billion. Adjusted EPS of $1.92 topped the $1.74 consensus, and Oracle raised its fiscal 2027 outlook to at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS.

Cash was the weak spot. Capital spending hit $28 billion, leaving free cash flow at negative $5 billion. Asked on the earnings call when free cash flow turns positive, CFO Hilary Maxson said: "We haven't given a particular time frame on that yet, and we don't expect to give that today." Oracle still plans $90 billion to $95 billion of capital spending this fiscal year.

Then on September 24, Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the Blue Owl (OWL:NYSE) unit building Project Jupiter, its New Mexico campus, citing potential delays in securing power. Oracle stock fell 3.5% that day, and its five-year credit default swaps (the cost of insuring its debt against default) hit a record. On October 22, Oracle said a Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) fuel-cell microgrid of up to 2.45 gigawatts would replace the site's planned gas turbines and diesel generators. That same day, Reuters reported Oracle's swaps were again close to a record.

title: Why Are Investors Buying Credit Default Swaps to Hedge AI-Related Debt?

Why Are Investors Buying Credit Default Swaps to Hedge AI-Related Debt?
Fiona Craig

GOOG

Trading disclosure
What is driving increased demand for credit default swaps?

Investors are increasing their use of credit default swaps (CDS) to hedge exposure to debt issued by companies involved in artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to market data and financial industry research.

The increase comes as technology companies raise substantial amounts of capital to finance data centres, semiconductors and other computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley Research reported that weekly trading in CDS linked to bonds issued by Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta (NASDAQ:META), Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) averaged more than $9 billion in September.

That compares with less than $2 billion per week in July.

Separately, Bloomberg data showed that trading volumes in US corporate CDS indices have already exceeded the total recorded throughout 2025.

The increase reflects greater demand for instruments that can provide protection against credit losses or allow investors to express views on changes in corporate credit risk.

How much debt have AI-related companies issued in 2026?

According to Morgan Stanley, AI-linked debt issuance reached an estimated $466 billion so far in 2026, compared with $101 billion during the corresponding period of 2025.

The increase has been driven by financing requirements for artificial intelligence infrastructure, including data centres, chips and associated computing systems.

Companies involved in developing and operating these facilities have accessed bond markets and other credit sources to support their investment programmes.

The expansion in borrowing has also increased investor attention on the relationship between upfront capital expenditure and the revenue that infrastructure projects may generate over time.

As debt issuance grows, investors are assessing how financing costs, operating performance and the financial relationships between AI companies could affect creditworthiness.

How do credit default swaps work?

A credit default swap is a financial derivative that provides protection against specified credit events, such as a default by a corporate borrower.

The buyer of protection makes payments to the seller in exchange for compensation if a covered credit event occurs, subject to the contract's terms.

CDS prices are generally expressed as a spread in basis points, with 100 basis points equivalent to one percentage point annually.

For example, a CDS spread of 108 basis points represents an annual premium of approximately $108,000 to protect $10 million of debt, assuming a conventional running-premium structure.

Lenders fund borrowers such as Oracle, CoreWeave and SpaceX, which use that financing to purchase chips from suppliers including Nvidia.

For Nvidia, the financing surge is supporting chip purchases across the ecosystem, analysts at IO Fund said.

Artificial intelligence is becoming a financeable infrastructure asset class as companies increasingly turn to debt markets to fund data centers and AI hardware, according to IO Fund.

Morgan Stanley data cited by IO Fund shows AI-related debt issuance reached $466 billion through September, up from $101 billion during the same period in 2025. Goldman Sachs puts the figure at $489 billion as of July 22, already above the $322 billion raised throughout 2025.

Nvidia shares closed 0.6% lower on Friday, Oracle shares closed 0.5% higher, while CoreWeave shares fell more than 2%.

What The AI Debt Boom Means For NVDA, ORCL and CRWV

IO Fund's analysis shows Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Oracle Corp. (ORCL) and CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) occupy different positions in the debt-funded AI infrastructure chain.

Lenders fund borrowers such as Oracle, CoreWeave and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX), which use that financing to purchase chips from suppliers including Nvidia. The borrowers then rent compute capacity to customers, while suppliers collect payment when chips are delivered.

For Nvidia, the financing surge is supporting chip purchases across the ecosystem, analysts at IO Fund said. Nvidia generated $127 billion in free cash flow over the 12 months ended July 2026, IO Fund noted. It also added that Nvidia has signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR targeting more than $500 billion in third-party capital.

CEO Jensen Huang said Nvidia retains the option to backstop up to $125 billion across these structures. IO Fund also notes that borrowers pay Nvidia and other chip suppliers upfront while customer revenue arrives over multi-year contracts.

"AI compute is becoming a financeable infrastructure asset class," IO Fund said.

For Oracle, the debt burden is already visible in its financials, IO Fund stated, while adding that Oracle reported $125.3 billion in notes payable and borrowings in the first quarter (Q1). This is over three times its $37.1 billion in cash and marketable securities. Quarterly interest expense rose 55% year over year to $1.43 billion.

Jefferies analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith lowered the firm's price target on Bloom Energy to $242 from $289 while maintaining a 'Hold' rating on the shares.

BTIG added that the cost of expanding manufacturing capacity is weighing on Bloom Energy's margin outlook.

Bloom Energy Reports Record Q3 Revenue

Bloom Energy reported record third-quarter revenue of $1.24 billion on Thursday, up 138.1% year over year, with product revenue rising 179.4% to $1.07 billion.

Gross margin increased to 33.8% from 29.2% a year earlier, while operating income rose to $225.4 million from $7.8 million. Its adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.94, compared with 15 cents a year earlier.

title: Can Manhattan Associates Stock Compound Your Money?

Can Manhattan Associates Stock Compound Your Money?

Manhattan Associates (MANH) stock has returned 59.7% since July 24, 2026, compared with 3.7% for the S&P 500. In the year before that run, the company kept buying back its own shares. It finished its latest four quarters with 59.0 million diluted shares, down from 62.4 million three years earlier. This reduction leaves each remaining share with a larger stake in the business. So how much has the shrinking share count added to what each of your shares earns?

Manhattan Associates' Earnings Per Share Outgrew Net Income

A shrinking share count has helped earnings per share grow faster than net income. Over the three years to June 2026, earnings per share climbed 14.6% a year, while net income increased 12.9% a year. Although the number of shares an investor holds remains the same, each one claims a larger portion of the profit.

In the past year, the buyback softened a decline instead. Net income fell 4.9% during the four quarters to June 2026, but earnings per share dropped a smaller 2.5%. Over those four quarters, the company spent $321 million more on buybacks than it issued in stock pay. That difference equals 2.3% of its market value at the October 22 close.

What Pays For Manhattan Associates' Buyback?

Most of this activity is funded by spare cash from a profitable software business. Over its latest four quarters, Manhattan Associates recorded an operating margin of 25.1%, compared with 18.5% for the S&P 500. Cash from operations reached $415 million, twice its net income. Capital spending consumed just 3.8% of that cash, leaving almost all of it as free cash flow.

The business generating that cash is still growing. Cloud revenue rose 26% to $127 million in fiscal Q2 2026. On the July 28, 2026 call, management said revenue already under contract but not yet booked reached $2.47 billion, up 23% from a year earlier.

Can Manhattan Associates Keep Buying Back At This Pace?

Not from free cash flow alone. Over the past four quarters, free cash flow covered 0.92 times the $435 million spent on buybacks, and the company paid no dividend. The rest came from its cash, which dropped to $186 million at the end of June 2026 from $231 million a year earlier. Even so, cash still exceeds debt by $132 million.

Each repurchased share also comes at a high price: the stock trades at 67.7 times earnings, compared with 23.0 for the S&P 500. As a result, every dollar spent retires a smaller slice of the company than it would at a lower price. The $225 million left under its share repurchase authority at the July 28 call would buy about 930,000 shares at the October 22 close of $242.17. In July, management also lowered its full-year GAAP operating margin forecast to 24.3% at the midpoint, down from 24.8%. This means a smaller share of each sales dollar is expected to remain as profit to pay for those purchases.

title: Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?
detail:
Bloom Energy Stock Sinks Despite Record Revenue and a Stellar Outlook. Is It Time to Buy?

NVDA

Trading disclosure

Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) delivered another blowout quarter, smashing estimates and growing profits faster than sales. Yet, its stock plunged after earnings and was down more than 12% as of Friday noon.

The company sells solid-oxide fuel cell servers that turn natural gas into electricity right at a customer's site. Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers desperately need that because the existing grid needs years to build additional capacity.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Bloom Energy can bypass the grid and swiftly deliver clean, reliable, 24/7 power to hyperscalers and data center operators. It delivered a complete fuel-cell system to Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) in 55 days last year. The tech giant was so impressed that it expanded its partnership for up to 2.8 gigawatts (GW) earlier this year.

So, what is happening with Bloom Energy stock? Why is it dropping like a rock – down 30% in one month, as of this writing?

Image source: Getty Images.

A bumper quarter and 2027 outlook

Revenue soared 138% year over year to a record $1.2 billion in the third quarter. Product sales, the fuel cell systems Bloom Energy ships to customers, topped $1 billion in sales in a single quarter for the first time.

Profit grew even faster. Adjusted operating margin jumped to 23.1% from 8.9% as revenue more than doubled while operating expenses rose only 26%. CFO Simon Edwards added that operating income in this single quarter surpassed what Bloom earned in all of 2025.

Then management raised its full-year revenue outlook for the third time this year. It now expects 2026 revenue of $4.5 billion, or about 122% growth.

Here's the kicker: Earlier in the year, Bloom Energy was guiding for a "humble" 60% revenue growth for the year. It has more than doubled its trajectory in just a couple of quarters.

So what's hurting the stock? The only metric I could find that may have miffed investors is cash burn. Bloom Energy posted negative free cash flow of $181 million in Q3.

Should investors worry? Hardly, because context is everything.

Is Bloom Energy stock a buy?

Demand is exploding, so Bloom Energy spent $153 million last quarter to scale up capacity as fast as possible. Data centers are built in phases, and Bloom is ready with its servers at each phase so operators don't have to wait.

That speed is everything for data centers.
